title: The Woman Who Ran the Rebellion: Tungasuca, the Letters, and the Plaza de Armas
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pampamarca, the birth the state commemorates
stops.date_confidence: traditional, contested against Tamburco
stops.campa: Micaela Bastidas Puyucahua is born on the twenty-third of June, 1744, in Pampamarca, a town of the province of Canas standing at three thousand eight hundred metres, some twelve and a half thousand feet above the sea. Her parents are Manuel Bastidas and Josefa Puyucahua. Some accounts call the family indigenous, others mestizo. No baptismal register has been produced by anyone who claims the town. The Peruvian state carves the name of Pampamarca on monuments and prints it in school texts on the strength of tradition alone.
suggested_refs: Parish records of Pampamarca, Canas: no baptismal entry for 1744 located

stops.name: Tamburco, the rival cradle
stops.date_confidence: traditional, contested against Pampamarca
stops.campa: Two hundred kilometres west, beyond the Apurimac, the town of Tamburco outside Abancay holds the same birth as its own. Regional biographers of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries put her cradle here, daughter of a Spanish father and an indigenous mother, and cite no document for it. The Pampamarca version, carried by nationalist historiography and by the state that raises the statues, has taken the textbooks. Neither town has produced a parish record, and both teach the birth as fact.
suggested_refs: Regional Apurimac biographical tradition placing the birth at Tamburco

stops.name: Surimana, the marriage in the church of the Purification
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of May, 1760, in the church of Nuestra Senora de la Purificacion at Surimana, Micaela Bastidas marries Jose Gabriel Condorcanqui. She is fifteen, a month short of sixteen; he is twenty-two, born in March of 1738. His family holds the caciazgo of this town and two others and traces itself to the last Sapa Inca of Vilcabamba, garroted by the Spanish in 1572. Biographies say the marriage register survives. The sources reachable here attest the temple and the date, not the book.
suggested_refs: Iglesia de Nuestra Senora de la Purificacion, Surimana, Canas

stops.name: Surimana, the three sons
stops.date_confidence: inferred from residence; birth towns undocumented
stops.campa: Hipolito is born in 1761, Mariano in 1762, Fernando in 1768. No register names the town of any of the three births; the household is fixed between Surimana and Tungasuca in these years and tradition divides the sons between them. Hipolito will be killed in front of his mother at twenty. Mariano will be pardoned, pensioned at six hundred pesos, arrested again, deported, and will die in Brazil in 1784. Fernando, ten years old on the day of the executions, will be shipwrecked off Portugal, jailed at Cadiz, and will die destitute in Madrid in 1798.
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the Condorcanqui-Bastidas sons across the Atlantic after 1781

stops.name: Tungasuca, the caciazgo and the mule trains
stops.date_confidence: contested: 1764 in the Bastidas articles, 1766 in the Tupac Amaru II article
stops.campa: Jose Gabriel succeeds to the caciazgo of Surimana, Tungasuca and Pampamarca, and the household settles at Tungasuca, a market town on the royal road running from Cusco to the southern altiplano. Micaela runs its economy: mule trains, coca and cloth, debts extended across the province and collected. For sixteen years this plaza and this market are the fixed point of the family's business. From this house she will direct the logistics of a rising that reaches from Cusco toward La Paz.
suggested_refs: The house attributed to the family on the plaza of Tungasuca

stops.name: Tinta, the seat of the corregimiento
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the family's documented trade
stops.campa: Tinta, seat of the corregimiento of Canas y Canchis, is where the family's trade meets colonial power across a desk. The corregidor Antonio de Arriaga collects tribute here, enforces the reparto, the forced purchase of goods at prices the buyer does not set, and draws the levies of men for the mines. Micaela and her husband come through on business through the seventeen seventies. They learn the offices and the size of the guard years before either of them has a use for the knowledge.
suggested_refs: Colonial administrative records of the corregimiento of Canas y Canchis

stops.name: Cerro Rico de Potosi, the mountain the levy feeds
stops.date_confidence: contextual, not a documented visit
stops.campa: Six hundred kilometres south stands the mountain the mita feeds. The draft that empties Canas and Canchis of its men delivers them to the Cerro Rico of Potosi, and the revolt Micaela will help lead is in large part a revolt against this silver. Ana de Urinza and Eustaquia de Souza had walked these streets armed a century before her, dressed as men, their portraits inscribed peruanas de Potosi. Simon Bolivar will climb to the summit in 1825 and plant three republican flags on it, forty-four years after her death.
suggested_refs: The mita de Potosi and its levy on the provinces of Canas y Canchis

stops.name: Tinta, the corregidor seized
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the fourth of November, 1780, Jose Gabriel Condorcanqui's men take the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga by ambush and carry him off under guard. The act is not yet rebellion in law: it is the arrest of a crown official by a cacique who claims descent from the Inca and who says he moves against bad government, not against the king. Micaela is at Tungasuca, where the prisoner is brought and held under guard. Six days stand between the seizure and the killing, and the province spends them waiting.
suggested_refs: The ambush and arrest of Antonio de Arriaga, 4 November 1780

stops.name: Tungasuca, Arriaga hanged in the plaza
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the tenth of November, in the plaza of Tungasuca, Arriaga is tried and publicly hanged before the town. His body is afterward carried to Tinta and buried in the church there, which is how the two towns come to be confused in the record: many accounts put the gallows at Tinta on the fourth. The scaffold stands in the square Micaela crosses daily, at the door of the house she keeps. Hanging a crown officer is a capital crime to which no pardon attaches.
suggested_refs: The plaza of Tungasuca, site of Arriaga's execution, 10 November 1780

stops.name: Tungasuca, the bando of the sixteenth
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of November, from Tungasuca, Jose Gabriel takes the name Tupac Amaru II and issues a bando decreeing the emancipation of the enslaved Africans and Afro-Peruvians of the province; the decrees of these weeks strike also at the reparto, the mita and the customs house. The town becomes the headquarters of a war: couriers at all hours, powder mixed in the yards, cloth cut for uniforms. Micaela signs the orders that move it, and the grievance of one family is now the programme of a province.
suggested_refs: The Tungasuca bando of 16 November 1780 emancipating the enslaved

stops.name: Sangarara, the church burns
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of November a rebel army of some six thousand breaks a royalist force of about two thousand three hundred at Sangarara and burns the church into which the soldiers and townspeople have crowded. Between three hundred ninety-five and five hundred seventy-six royalists die. Micaela is not on the field. She is at Tungasuca, moving provisions and men toward it. Bishop Moscoso y Peralta excommunicates Tupac Amaru for the burning; whether the sentence names her too is not attested anywhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The burned church of Sangarara, 18 November 1780

stops.name: Tungasuca, constituted jefa interina
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment; day within the month inferred
stops.campa: After the victory at Sangarara she is constituted jefa interina of the rebellion, interim chief, and takes her seat in the council of five that governs it. The title is not honorific. Her husband is in the field; the headquarters, the treasury, the recruitment and the discipline are hers. She signs safe-conducts, orders deserters punished, and writes to caciques across the southern sierra in the name of the Inca. Her colonial accusers will charge her, in the word they choose, with a resolucion varonil.
stops.quote_source: The charge levelled by her colonial accusers, quoted in Mary G. Berg, 'Micaela Bastidas y su época' (Ledizioni, 2013)
suggested_refs: Mary G. Berg, 'Micaela Bastidas y su epoca', in Irina Bajini (ed.), Ledizioni 2013, pp. 125-130

stops.name: Tungasuca, the letter that calls him back from Yauri
stops.date_confidence: attested letter, undated in the transcription
stops.campa: Her husband is south, moving slowly through the towns, two days lost at Yauri. She writes. The letter is captured with the rest of her papers and will be read back to her at trial as evidence that she commanded rather than followed. She warns that the royalists are arming, that the men are drifting home, that the delay is the whole danger. Her repeated warnings turn him back from the southern campaign at Lampa in December. She calls him Chepe, which is what she has called him since she was fifteen.
stops.quote: Chepe mío, tú me has de acabar de pesadumbres, pues andas muy despacio paseándote en los pueblos y mas en Yauri, tardándote dos grandes días con gran descuido.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Túpac Amaru II, transcribed on es.wikisource, citing Congreso del Perú, Fondo Editorial Bicentenario, 'Túpac Amaru' vol. 6, p. 368
suggested_refs: The captured correspondence of Micaela Bastidas, entered as evidence by the Areche tribunal
sources: es.wikisource, 'Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Tupac Amaru II'

stops.name: Yanaoca, the muster on the road
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no document names her here
stops.campa: Yanaoca, market town of Canas between Tungasuca and the southern road, gathers recruits and provisions before they move north toward the front. No surviving letter puts Micaela in this square. What the record carries is the volume of traffic the rising generates along this corridor: grain, coca, powder and men, moving under written directions that are increasingly hers. The town is entered here as tradition, one stop on a route she is documented to have governed without necessarily walking it.
suggested_refs: The Canas muster routes of December 1780, reconstructed from campaign geography
sources: Inferred from campaign geography; no specific document

stops.name: Combapata, the supply road north
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no document names her here
stops.campa: Combapata sits on the royal road between Tinta and Cusco, at a river crossing every rebel column and every royalist patrol must use. Supply trains organised from Tungasuca pass through it through December and into January, carrying grain and powder toward the army gathering below Cusco. No document places Micaela at this crossing in person; the stop is inference from the shape of the road, and is offered as that. Royalist columns will use the same crossing in April, moving the other way.
suggested_refs: The royal road crossing at Combapata, Canchis
sources: Inferred from campaign road geography; no specific document

stops.name: Quiquijana, a day's ride from the city
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no document names her here
stops.campa: Quiquijana, in Quispicanchi, marks the road drawing in on Cusco itself, within a day's ride of the city the rebel army is about to invest. Reinforcements and supplies organised from the rear pass through it toward the camp in the hills above the city. No document names her at this crossing. What is documented is the administration behind the traffic, run from Tungasuca in her hand, and the stop rests on the logistics of the siege rather than on her footsteps.
suggested_refs: The Quispicanchi stretch of the royal road, approach to Cusco
sources: Inferred from siege-era supply geography; no specific document

stops.name: Urcos, the lake on the last approach
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no document names her here
stops.campa: Urcos, beside its lake, is the last substantial town on the southern road before the passes open into the valley of the Inca capital. Rebel columns and their supply trains cross it in force in the first days of January, and will cross it again in reverse within the month. No source places Micaela here. The town is unavoidable geography for anyone moving between Tinta and Cusco in these months, whether under orders or under escort, and she will come this way herself in April, in chains.
suggested_refs: The lake road at Urcos, final approach to Cusco from the south
sources: Inferred from siege-era supply and later captivity route geography

segments.name: The Siege That Is Not Pressed

stops.name: Cusco, the camp above San Sebastian
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The mobilisation order goes out on the fourth of January, and the rebel army camps in the hills above Cusco, near San Sebastian and the approaches later called Picchu. Tupac Amaru declines to storm the city, unwilling to spend indigenous lives against a garrison that has placed indigenous fighters in its own front rank. Micaela is not at this camp. She is at Tungasuca, watching the siege stall by messenger, and it is from there that she writes the letters for which she is best remembered.
stops.quote: Estamos en medio de los enemigos, no tenemos segura la vida y por tu causa a pique de peligrar todos mis hijos, los demás de nuestra parte.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Túpac Amaru II, transcribed on es.wikisource, citing Congreso del Perú, Fondo Editorial Bicentenario, 'Túpac Amaru' vol. 6
suggested_refs: The rebel siege lines above San Sebastian, January 1781

stops.name: Tungasuca, the letter about the soldiers going home
stops.date_confidence: attested letter, undated in the transcription
stops.campa: The army before Cusco is thinning while its commander waits. She writes that the soldiers are right to be sick of it and to go back each to his own town, which is not a complaint about the soldiers. It is an accounting. Men who are not fed and not used will leave, and a rebellion that cannot hold its men has already lost the thing it is made of. She keeps the ledger of the war: what is sent, what arrives, what walks away. The city has not been taken and the reinforcements from Lima are already marching.
stops.quote: los soldados tienen razón de aburrirse irse cada uno a sus pueblo.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Túpac Amaru II, transcribed on es.wikisource, citing Congreso del Perú, Fondo Editorial Bicentenario, 'Túpac Amaru' vol. 6
suggested_refs: The Wikisource transcription of the captured letter, marked incomplete by its editors
sources: es.wikisource, 'Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Tupac Amaru II'

stops.name: Tungasuca, the letter of no more patience
stops.date_confidence: attested letter, undated in the transcription
stops.campa: She writes that she has no patience left, that she is capable of giving herself up to the enemy to have her life taken from her, because she sees how little urgency he brings to a matter that is eating all their lives. She writes that no life among them is safe any longer, and that through his delay her own sons stand directly in the way of what is coming for all of them. She writes as a commander to a commander, from ninety kilometres away, about a campaign she can see being lost from there.
stops.quote: Yo ya no tengo paciencia para aguantar todo esto, pues yo misma soy capaz de entregarme a los enemigos para que me quiten la vida, porque veo el poco anhelo con que ves este asunto tan grave que corroe con detrimento la vida de todos.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Túpac Amaru II, transcribed on es.wikisource, citing Congreso del Perú, Fondo Editorial Bicentenario, 'Túpac Amaru' vol. 6, p. 368
suggested_refs: The captured correspondence as the principal documentary basis for her command role
sources: es.wikisource, 'Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Tupac Amaru II'

stops.name: Cusco, the siege lifted
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: About a week of fighting before the walls, and on the eleventh of January the siege is lifted and the insurgents scatter. Spanish reinforcements have arrived in the interval the delay bought them. She had told him what the delay would cost, in writing, more than once, and the letters saying so are in a satchel that will be captured with her in April and read aloud in a courtroom in this city. By March the rebel army will be seven thousand strong again; it will never stand before Cusco a second time.
stops.quote: Bastante advertencia te di, para que inmediatamente fueses al Cuzco pero has dado todo a la barata, dándoles tiempo para que se prevengan como ya lo han hecho.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Túpac Amaru II, transcribed on es.wikisource, citing Congreso del Perú, Fondo Editorial Bicentenario, 'Túpac Amaru' vol. 6, p. 368
suggested_refs: The lifting of the siege of Cusco, 11 January 1781
sources: es.wikisource, 'Carta de Micaela Bastidas a Tupac Amaru II'

stops.name: Tinta, the last muster of the province
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no source places her here
stops.campa: By April the royalist curaca Mateo Pumacahua is advancing on Tinta and the Canas y Canchis heartland with some two thousand indigenous troops loyal to the crown. The tradition has Micaela organising what defence the province can still raise, from the same district where the rising opened five months before. No source checked places her at Tinta in these days; the Spanish record has her already moving, and this stop is carried as tradition. The army that took Sangarara is scattered, worn out and short of powder.
suggested_refs: Pumacahua's royalist offensive of April 1781 in Canas y Canchis

stops.name: Checacupe, the army broken
stops.date_confidence: attested; fighting 5-6 April
stops.campa: On the fifth and sixth of April the remaining rebel force is beaten at Checacupe, and in the confusion two men Tupac Amaru has trusted turn against him: Ventura Landaeta and Francisco Santa Cruz. The defeat scatters what is left of the rebel command into the passes south of Tinta. Micaela's presence at this engagement is not documented by name. She is travelling with or near the retreating family group in these days, on the strength of the accounts that describe her capture within the same forty-eight hours.
suggested_refs: The rebel defeat at Checacupe, 5-6 April 1781

stops.name: Langui, Tupac Amaru taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixth of April Tupac Amaru is seized at Langui, handed to the royalists by Landaeta and Santa Cruz after the defeat at Checacupe. Mateo Pumacahua, who commanded the offensive that broke the rebellion, takes the fame and the prestige of the capture without having made it; his own file is careful about the distinction. English accounts place the seizure between Tinta and Sangarara, which is nowhere near it. The town is Langui, on its lake, in the province of Canas.
suggested_refs: The seizure at Langui, 6 April 1781, by Ventura Landaeta and Francisco Santa Cruz

stops.name: Langui, the seventh of April: Micaela handed over
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia; the majority tradition has her taken with her husband on the sixth
stops.campa: On the seventh of April the same Landaeta delivers Micaela Bastidas to the royalists. She is taken separately from her husband, one day later, while attempting to get south toward La Paz. The version in wider circulation has the whole family run to ground together at Langui on the sixth. The two accounts are not reconciled in the sources and are both carried here. Either way she is in the hands of the crown before the week is out, and the satchel of her letters is in them too.
suggested_refs: The road south toward La Paz, on which she was taken

segments.name: The Royal Road Northward, in Chains

stops.name: Combapata, the column marched north
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the fixed geography of the road
stops.campa: In the days after Langui the prisoners are marched north under heavy escort along the same royal road their own supply trains used through the winter: Tupac Amaru, Micaela, the sons, the captured captains. Chroniclers describe the captives roped or chained and watched by crowds in towns that had cheered the rising four months earlier. No itinerary survives naming every halt. The route is reconstructed from what the road forces on any march between Langui and the city, which is not in dispute.
suggested_refs: Chronicle accounts of the captivity march from Langui to Cusco
sources: Reconstructed from royal road geography; general chronicle accounts

stops.name: Checacupe, back across the broken field
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the fixed geography of the road
stops.campa: The column passes back through Checacupe, where the army was broken days before, now empty of any force that could intervene. Contemporary accounts note the weight the colonial authorities attach to marching the captured family past the sites of their own campaign, showing every town on the road what the collapse looks like. The halt itself is reconstruction rather than record. The route is not contested by historians of the campaign, since the column had no other road north.
suggested_refs: The symbolic routing of the captivity march past the rebellion's own battlefields
sources: Reconstructed from royal road geography; general chronicle accounts

stops.name: Acomayo, the doubtful branch
stops.date_confidence: weakly attested; a flagged possibility, not a settled stop
stops.campa: Acomayo lies off the direct Tinta road but inside the province the rising convulsed, and appears in some reconstructions of the captivity march as a parallel route used to avoid ambush or to gather further prisoners on the way. The evidence for it is thinner than for the towns on the royal road itself. It is entered here as a documented possibility and nothing firmer, one of several villages colonial officers may have used to consolidate captives before the last approach to Cusco.
suggested_refs: Regional accounts of an alternate captivity-march route through Acomayo
sources: Weakly attested alternate-route hypothesis; no primary document

stops.name: Urcos, the crowds on the lake road
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the fixed geography of the road
stops.campa: The column reaches Urcos again, this time as captives rather than as an army's supply line, within a day's march of Cusco. Chroniclers describe crowds gathering along the lakeside road to watch the prisoners pass, some in sympathy, many compelled or merely curious under a heavy Spanish guard. It is the last substantial town before the final approach to the city where the family will be tried, and where, within five weeks, most of them will be killed in public.
suggested_refs: The lake road at Urcos, retraced under guard in April 1781
sources: Reconstructed from royal road geography; general chronicle accounts

stops.name: San Jeronimo, the bells of Cusco
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: At San Jeronimo, on the eastern approach, accounts have the cathedral bells of Cusco already ringing in celebration days before the column itself arrives. Tupac Amaru rides chained on a mule, his face described by hostile chroniclers as unnervingly composed. Micaela's bearing on this approach is not separately described in the surviving accounts, which fix their attention on her husband. Her presence in the same column and under the same guard is not disputed by anyone.
suggested_refs: Chronicle accounts of the entry of the captives into Cusco, April 1781

stops.name: Cusco, the cells by the Capilla de San Ignacio
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to the building; the detention itself attested
stops.campa: The captured leaders are held for interrogation in cells associated with the Capilla de San Ignacio and the colegio beside it, under the authority of the visitador general Jose Antonio de Areche, sent from Lima with sweeping powers to end the rising and make an example of its end. Conditions are harsh and torture is applied to extract confessions and names. The sources are far fuller on her husband's treatment than on hers; her confinement is documented in general terms only, which is itself the record.
suggested_refs: The Capilla de San Ignacio and the colegio complex, Cusco, used as detention in 1781

stops.name: Cusco, her own letters read back to her
stops.date_confidence: attested for the tribunal; the day within the month inferred
stops.campa: Before Areche's tribunal she is questioned over several days on the extent of the conspiracy, its money and the names of its sympathisers in Cusco and beyond. Her captured letters are read back to her as evidence of command, not of loyalty. When Areche offers pardon to those who will denounce Tupac Amaru, he writes the exception into the document by name, and the name he writes is hers. In the charges her firmness is called varonil, manly, which is the nearest word the court has for it.
stops.quote: la muger del Rebelde Micaela Bastidas
stops.quote_source: José Antonio de Areche, excluding her by name from the offered pardon; quoted in Mary G. Berg, 'Micaela Bastidas y su época' (Ledizioni, 2013)
suggested_refs: The Areche tribunal record and the captured Bastidas correspondence entered as evidence

stops.name: Cusco, the sentence
stops.date_confidence: contested: 14 May in the Bastidas article, 15 May in the rebellion article
stops.campa: Sentence is passed on Tupac Amaru, Micaela and the captured captains. One source dates it the fourteenth of May and another the fifteenth, so the condemned wait either four days or three; the arithmetic depends on a contradiction nobody has resolved. The punishments are designed for public terror: forced witness of one's family dying first, then dismemberment, then the distribution of the parts to the towns that rose. Areche's sentencia also bans Inca names, Inca dress, and the keeping of Inca genealogies.
suggested_refs: The sentencia of visitador general Jose Antonio de Areche, Cusco, May 1781
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Rebelion de Tupac Amaru II' (15 May)

stops.name: Cusco, Plaza de Armas: made to watch her son die
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of May, in the Plaza de Armas, she is made to watch the execution of her son Hipolito, whose tongue is cut out before he is hanged, and of Antonio Bastidas and the cacica Tomasa Tito Condemayta, who commanded troops as she did. The sequence is the tribunal's own design, the order of deaths chosen for what it will do to the woman kept alive to see them. The square is cleared of its market and ringed with troops. Hostile observers note her composure and write it down as defiance.
suggested_refs: Contemporary colonial chronicles of the executions of 18 May 1781

stops.name: Cusco, Plaza de Armas: the garrote that fails
stops.date_confidence: attested; the sequence and the final method differ between sources
stops.campa: Her tongue is cut out. The garrote will not take: the executioners judge her neck too thin for the mechanism. English accounts have them finish her with a rope and then with clubs and kicks to the stomach and the breasts; Spanish accounts keep the garrote and add the struggle. Both agree the machine failed and the men resorted to their hands. She is thirty-six, and she dies before her husband, who is killed in the same square within the hour. A sentence is attributed to her afterward; no contemporary document carries it.
stops.quote: Me perdí de ver a mis hijos seguir creciendo, todo por mi patria, por la igualdad y por la libertad.
stops.quote_source: Attributed final utterance, carried by es.wikipedia without a contemporary source; wording and moment both disputed
suggested_refs: The divergent chronicle accounts of the method of her execution

segments.name: The Body Scattered, the Name Multiplied

stops.name: Cusco, Huacaypata: the square keeps its accounts
stops.date_confidence: attested for both events; the pairing is the atlas reading
stops.campa: This square is Huacaypata, into which Francisco Pizarro rode in 1533 before stripping the gold from the Coricancha two streets away and installing a puppet Sapa Inca. Two hundred and forty-eight years separate his entry from her death on the same stones. Helena Blavatsky will ride through this valley in the next century and read its walls as the relics of a vanished race, which is one way of not seeing a rebellion. The plaza is a market again by the following week.
suggested_refs: The plaza constellation of essay 207; Huacaypata as recurring atlas location

stops.name: Cusco, the quartering and the dispersal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the practice; her own remains undocumented
stops.campa: The bodies are dismembered and the parts sent out to the towns that rose, so that the crown's reach can be seen from every plaza in the province. Tupac Amaru's head is displayed in Cusco and then sent to Tinta; his limbs go to Tungasuca, Ayapata, Livitaca and Santa Rosa, each destination named in the record. For Micaela the record names nothing. General accounts describe dismemberment and display without saying which town received which part of her. No grave and no tomb is documented anywhere.
suggested_refs: Areche's distribution order for the remains of the condemned, May 1781

stops.name: Tungasuca, the plaza taught the other lesson
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to her remains; the town's role attested for her husband's
stops.campa: Tungasuca, where the bando was read and where she ran the war for five months, is named among the destinations for the exhibited remains. The sources conflate her husband's documented limb with looser claims about the family, and the conflation is left standing here rather than resolved. The plaza where Arriaga was hanged in November receives, in June, whatever the tribunal has decided to send it, and the town is required to look at what arrives.
suggested_refs: Tungasuca as a named destination for the dispersed remains of 1781
sources: General accounts of remains distribution to former rebel strongholds

stops.name: Livitaca, the leg sent into the highlands
stops.date_confidence: attested for her husband's remains; her organising role there inferred
stops.campa: Livitaca, in the Chumbivilcas highlands, receives one of Tupac Amaru's legs as a warning to a province that had supplied him with men. Micaela's hand in that distant recruitment is not documented by name; it is inferred from the general reach of the administration she ran out of Tungasuca, which stretched well past the roads she is recorded travelling. The warning is aimed at people who had answered letters she signed. No distribution order names any part of her.
suggested_refs: The distribution of Tupac Amaru's remains to Livitaca, Chumbivilcas

stops.name: Cusco, Bolivar refuses the crown of the Incas
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Bolivar file; the tie back to 1781 is reconstruction
stops.campa: Forty-four years on, Simon Bolivar enters Cusco as a liberator and is offered the crown of the Incas. He refuses it and sends it to Sucre, then writes to his sister from the city the same month. Manuel Belgrano had already proposed, before Congress in July 1816, restoring the Inca dynasty with its capital at Cuzco: the stolen house restored. Neither man cites the couple killed in the plaza he is standing in. The cause they were quartered for is by now the founding argument of three republics.
suggested_refs: Bolivar's letters from Cusco, July 1825; Belgrano's Inca-restoration proposal of 6 July 1816

stops.name: Lima, the effigy in the Panteon de los Proceres
stops.date_confidence: attested for the effigy; date of installation unrecorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: An effigy of Micaela Bastidas stands in the Panteon de los Proceres in Lima, the capital that sent Areche south with his powers. Its exact position in the building could not be confirmed; the dedicated page returned an error. She is honoured in the city that condemned her, having no grave to be honoured in. Policarpa Salavarrieta, hanged by the same crown at Bogota in 1817 for the same kind of work, is likewise a national monument in a country that has no bones of hers either.
suggested_refs: The Panteon de los Proceres, Lima; page unreachable this session

stops.name: Cusco, Guevara reads the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Guevara file; the tie back to 1781 is reconstruction
stops.campa: Aime Tschiffely had ridden into this city in 1925 with two Criollo horses, on what he called the road the runners of the Inca used. Twenty-seven years later Ernesto Guevara arrives and calls Cusco the navel of the world, reading its walls and Sacsayhuaman as an accusation against the present rather than a ruin of the past. Neither traveller names Micaela Bastidas. Both are moving on the roads her couriers used, past the square where she was killed, in a country that has since named a university after her.
stops.quote: Cuzco: the one word that defines it exactly is evocation.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, 1952, as carried in working/journeys/che_guevara.journey.json
suggested_refs: The Inca road network as retraced by Tschiffely in 1925 and Guevara in 1952

stops.name: Ayrihuanca, a district takes her name
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: By Law 12861 of the twentieth of December, 1957, under President Manuel Prado Ugarteche, a district of the province of Grau in Apurimac is created and named Micaela Bastidas, its capital Ayrihuanca, at an average altitude of three thousand five hundred and ten metres. It is a hundred kilometres from Tamburco, one of the two towns that claim her birth. A republic that cannot produce her body draws her name on its own map instead, and the map is where she is buried.
suggested_refs: Ley 12861 of 20 December 1957 creating the Distrito de Micaela Bastidas

stops.name: Abancay, the university
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of September, 2000, Law 27348 creates the Universidad Nacional Micaela Bastidas de Apurimac at Abancay, in the province whose outlying town of Tamburco has claimed her birth for two centuries against Pampamarca. A plaza in the same city carries her name and a sculpture of her at its centre, though no portrait was ever made from life and every face given to her is an invention of the century that needed one. Peru had already put her on a postage stamp in 1971.
suggested_refs: Ley 27348 of 26 September 2000 creating UNAMBA at Abancay

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the park at Puerto Madero
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirty-first of January, 2003, a park of seven or eight hectares opens on the reclaimed docks of Puerto Madero in Buenos Aires and is named for her: an elevated walkway, a rose garden, sports grounds, forty thousand trees and shrubs, four thousand kilometres from the plaza where she was killed. In 1976 Peru had passed Law 21705 recognising the bicentenary of the rebellion under both their names. She has no tomb. She has a district, a university, a stamp, a law and a park.
suggested_refs: Parque Micaela Bastidas, Puerto Madero, opened 31 January 2003
